chapter_summary:
Before we can even think about deploying a Hyperledger Fabric network or writing chaincode, we need to ensure our local machine is equipped with the foundational tools that Fabric relies upon. Think of these prerequisites as the bedrock upon which your entire Fabric development experience will be built. Without them, you'll encounter errors and roadblocks at every turn. The core components we need are Docker and Docker Compose for containerization, Go and Node.js for chaincode and client application development, cURL for downloading resources, and Git for version control and cloning repositories.

Let's start with Docker. Hyperledger Fabric leverages Docker extensively for containerization. Every component of a Fabric network—peers, orderers, Certificate Authorities (CAs), CouchDB instances (if used for state database)—runs as a separate Docker container. This containerized approach provides isolation, portability, and simplifies deployment. Docker Compose, an extension of Docker, allows us to define and run multi-container Docker applications. Fabric networks, by their nature, are multi-container applications, so Docker Compose is indispensable for orchestrating the various services that make up a Fabric network, such as bringing up multiple peers, orderers, and CAs with a single command. Without Docker and Docker Compose, you wouldn't be able to run a local Fabric network at all. Ensure you have a recent version of Docker Engine (typically 18.03 or later) and Docker Compose (1.24.0 or later) installed.

Next, we need programming languages. Hyperledger Fabric supports chaincode development in several languages, primarily Go, Node.js, and Java. For this certification, we will primarily focus on Go and Node.js, as they are widely used in the Fabric community and are well-supported by the official samples. Go is often preferred for its performance characteristics and strong typing, while Node.js is popular for its asynchronous capabilities and extensive ecosystem, especially for client applications interacting with the blockchain. You'll need Go version 1.14.x or later and Node.js version 10.x or later (preferably LTS versions like 12.x, 14.x, or 16.x). It's crucial to set up your Go environment correctly, especially the `GOPATH` environment variable, which tells Go where to find your source code, packages, and compiled binaries. A common mistake is not setting `GOPATH` or setting it incorrectly, leading to `go get` or `go build` commands failing. For Node.js, ensure `npm` (Node Package Manager) is also installed, as it comes bundled with Node.js and is essential for managing dependencies in Node.js chaincode and client applications.

Beyond the core development languages, we also require `cURL` and `Git`. `cURL` is a command-line tool for transferring data with URLs. It's often used in shell scripts to download files, including the Hyperledger Fabric binaries and Docker images from remote repositories. While you could manually download files, `cURL` simplifies this process significantly, especially within automated setup scripts. `Git` is a distributed version control system. Hyperledger Fabric's official samples and documentation are hosted on GitHub, and `Git` is the primary tool we'll use to clone these repositories to our local machine. This allows us to access the `fabric-samples` repository, which contains the `test-network` and various chaincode examples, providing a starting point for our development.

Finally, while not strictly a Fabric prerequisite, having a good text editor or Integrated Development Environment (IDE) like VS Code is highly recommended. It will make writing and debugging chaincode and client applications much more efficient. For Python users, Python 3.x is also often used for utility scripts or specific client applications, though it's not a core requirement for Fabric itself unless you plan to use Python chaincode (which is less common than Go or Node.js). Always ensure your operating system is up-to-date, whether you're on Linux, macOS, or Windows, as this can prevent compatibility issues with newer software versions. Taking the time to correctly install and verify these prerequisites now will save you countless hours of troubleshooting later.

screens.title: Prerequisites for Hyperledger Fabric Development
screens.subtitle: What you must install and verify before you build or run Fabric networks and chaincode

narration.text: Before you write chaincode or bring up a Fabric test network, your local environment must have a small set of reliable tools. These prerequisites are the foundation for every development step: container tooling to run peers and orderers, language runtimes to compile and execute chaincode or client apps, and command-line utilities to fetch and manage samples. In practice that means Docker and Docker Compose for containers, Go and Node. js for chaincode and clients, plus cURL and Git to download and manage code. You’ll also set a Go workspace variable so the Go toolchain can find your code. Verifying each tool is installed and at a compatible version saves hours of debugging later. For example, if Docker is not running you cannot start any Fabric component; if GOPATH is unset, Go commands will fail to locate packages. This lesson will show you the expected tools, how to confirm them on your system, common mistakes to watch for, and a short verification activity so you can prove your setup is ready. By the end, you will be able to run simple version checks and recognize a handful of common installation failures.

keyIdea.title: Install & verify core tools
keyIdea.text: Successful Fabric development depends on a small, explicit set of tools: Docker, Docker Compose, Go, Node.js, cURL, and Git. Verify versions and environment variables before proceeding.

narration.text: These objectives focus your setup tasks and verification checks. Second, you will understand the role each tool plays in the Fabric ecosystem — for example, why Docker provides isolation for peers and why Docker Compose simplifies multi-service startups. Third, you will learn how to verify installation and correct versions for each tool so you can confirm your system is compatible before starting network operations. Being deliberate about these checks prevents many frustrating failures later when you try to launch a Fabric network or build chaincode.

screens.title: Why Docker and Docker Compose are required
screens.subtitle: Containerization and orchestration for Fabric components

narration.text: Docker and Docker Compose are central to running a Hyperledger Fabric network locally. Docker provides a lightweight, isolated runtime for each Fabric component — peers, orderers, Certificate Authorities and optional CouchDB instances — which prevents conflicts between services and allows you to mirror production-like deployments. Docker Compose complements this by letting you describe a multi-container application with a single YAML file. A Fabric test network often includes multiple peers across organizations, orderers, and CAs; Compose brings them up together in a reproducible configuration. For example, using the Fabric samples we can define four peers and two orderers in a compose file and start them with one command, which is essential for developer productivity. A common misconception is that Docker alone is enough to manage multi-service setups; without Compose you would need to start and link many containers manually. Another pitfall is mismatched versions: Fabric assumes recent Docker Engine and Compose versions, so verify your runtime meets the chapter’s minimums before proceeding. To summarize, Docker isolates components and Compose orchestrates them; both are required to run Fabric networks locally, and confirming they run correctly eliminates the most immediate source of "it won't start" errors.

keyIdea.title: Containers + orchestration
keyIdea.text: Docker gives isolation; Docker Compose defines and runs the multi-container Fabric topology in a reproducible way.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Docker & Compose
Definition

Containerization and orchestration

Docker runs each Fabric component in its own container for isolation and portability. Docker Compose defines how those containers start together to form a network.

Teaching points
  • Every peer, orderer, CA, and optional database runs as a container.
  • Compose collects service definitions, environment variables and volume mappings in one file.
  • Compose simplifies bringing up a reproducible test network for development.
Common mistake
Running containers manually without Compose leads to missing links and environment mismatches. Use Compose to avoid that drift.
Example
Sample workflow
Define services in a compose file, and run the compose command to start peers, orderers, and CAs together for development testing.
Why this matters

Using Docker and Compose reduces environmental variability so your local network behaves like a reproducible lab. This consistency is critical when you deploy chaincode or troubleshoot network failures.

Key Takeaway

Both Docker and Docker Compose are required to run and orchestrate a local Fabric network reliably.

screens.title: Verify Docker and Docker Compose
screens.subtitle: Run the basic checks that confirm container tooling is available and running

narration.text: Verifying your container tooling is a straightforward process but essential. First, confirm Docker is installed and the daemon is running. If the daemon is not running, container operations will fail even though the Docker binary may be present. Second, verify Docker Compose is installed and accessible; Compose versions older than the suggested minimum can be incompatible with Fabric sample compose files. When you run these checks, capture the version strings and any service information as proof. A simple practice is to run the Docker version command to view the Engine and client versions, and a Compose version command to check the tool’s release. If you see an error indicating the command is not found, check your PATH and the installation steps — sometimes the Compose binary uses a separate installation method. Also watch for permission or daemon errors: on some systems you must start the Docker service or add your user to a docker group. A misconception to avoid is trusting that installation alone means readiness; you must ensure the Docker daemon responds. After these checks you will be confident that the container runtime and orchestrator are ready to host Fabric components.

keyIdea.title: Confirm runtime & service
keyIdea.text: A present Docker binary is not enough; the Docker daemon must be running and Docker Compose must be on your PATH and at a compatible version.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Verify Docker
Checks to run
docker --version
docker-compose --version
docker info
Interpretation
  • If you see version strings, the binaries are present.
  • Docker info shows the daemon status and running containers; errors here indicate the service needs to start.
  • Compose must be compatible with your Docker Engine; older Compose can fail with complex Fabric compose files.
Troubleshooting
  • "Command not found" — check PATH and installation directories.
  • Daemon errors — start the Docker service or confirm permissions for the current user.
  • Compose compatibility — install a Compose version at or above the minimum recommended for your Fabric samples.
Pro tip

If installations succeed but networks fail to start, first confirm Docker info shows the daemon healthy before debugging Fabric-specific errors.

screens.title: Go for chaincode: versions and GOPATH
screens.subtitle: Why Go is commonly used and how GOPATH affects your builds

narration.text: Go is a statically typed, compiled language frequently used for Hyperledger Fabric chaincode because of its performance and straightforward compilation model. For Fabric development we expect Go at or above the chapter’s recommended baseline. A crucial part of using Go is setting the GOPATH environment variable, which defines the root of your Go workspace where the toolchain locates source code, downloaded packages and compiled binaries. If GOPATH is unset or incorrect, commands that fetch or build packages will fail, producing confusing errors about missing packages. A common practical step is to set GOPATH to a directory in your home folder and add its bin subdirectory to your PATH so installed tools are reachable. For example, you might export the GOPATH and update your shell profile so the change persists. A misconception is that modern module-aware Go eliminates GOPATH entirely; while modules change dependency handling, Fabric samples and older workflows still rely on a correctly configured workspace in some cases. Always check the sample repository guidance. In short: install a recent Go runtime, set GOPATH so the toolchain can find code, and verify with a version check and a test build to ensure chaincode compilation will work.

keyIdea.title: GOPATH and Go runtime
keyIdea.text: Go compiles chaincode; GOPATH must be set so the Go toolchain can find your workspace and packages when building.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Go & GOPATH
Why Go

Go is commonly used for Fabric chaincode because it compiles to fast binaries and presents strong typing. For chaincode development you need a compatible Go runtime installed and a workspace where your chaincode and dependencies live.

GOPATH explained

GOPATH is an environment variable that points to your Go workspace where go get, go build and other tools expect to find source and binaries. If it is unset, you may see errors when fetching or compiling packages.

Common mistake

Not setting GOPATH or forgetting to add GOPATH/bin to PATH causes go get or go build failures. Double-check your shell profile.

Quick verification
go version echo $GOPATH # on Linux/macOS echo %GOPATH% # on Windows CMD
Interpretation
  • Go version confirms runtime availability.
  • The GOPATH echo command shows your workspace location; set it if empty.
  • Add GOPATH/bin to PATH so installed tools are executable from your shell.

screens.title: Node.js and npm — role and verification
screens.subtitle: How Node.js complements Go and how to confirm Node and npm are ready

narration.text: Node. js is an important runtime in the Fabric ecosystem because it supports JavaScript chaincode and rich client applications that interact with the blockchain asynchronously. Compared with Go, Node. js offers an extensive package ecosystem and rapid development cycles, making it a common choice for client applications. When you install Node. js it usually includes npm, the package manager, which you use to install dependencies for client apps and sometimes JavaScript chaincode. Verifying Node and npm is a simple two-step check: confirm the Node runtime is present and confirm npm can list its version. A common example is installing a client SDK package for Fabric; npm must be available to fetch and manage the SDK. A misconception is that chaincode must be Go — Node. js chaincode is supported and often used for JavaScript-centric teams. If npm is missing after installing Node, the install method may have been incomplete or PATH may not include the installation directory. In practice, verify both Node and npm are present before attempting to install or run JavaScript chaincode or client examples. Node.js and npm — role and verification means node provides the javascript runtime and npm manages packages; both are needed when using js chaincode or sdks for client apps.. In practical terms, how node.js complements go and how to confirm node and npm are ready. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node.js for JavaScript chaincode and clients
keyIdea.text: Node provides the JavaScript runtime and npm manages packages; both are needed when using JS chaincode or SDKs for client apps.

Role comparison
Go
Preferred for high-performance chaincode and strong typing.
Node.js
Popular for client apps and JavaScript chaincode due to rich npm ecosystem.
Verification
node --version
npm --version
Common pitfalls
  • Installing Node but not npm — confirm both commands return versions.
  • Using outdated Node LTS versions may still work, but prefer an LTS recommended by the community for stability.
  • When installing SDK dependencies, run npm install in the project directory so package.json is respected.
Key Takeaway

Confirm both the Node runtime and npm are present when working with JavaScript chaincode or Fabric client libraries.

screens.title: cURL and Git: download and code management
screens.subtitle: Why these CLI tools are essential for fetching Fabric binaries and samples

narration.text: cURL and Git are simple but indispensable command-line tools for Fabric development. cURL downloads files and is commonly used in setup scripts to fetch Fabric binaries and Docker images. It makes scripted installation reproducible so you do not manually download files. Git is the tool used to clone the fabric-samples repository and manage changes to your development code. The fabric-samples repository contains the test network and chaincode examples you will work with. Verifying both tools is quick: run the version command for each and ensure the commands return sensible outputs. An important practical tip is to clone fabric-samples into a predictable workspace so scripts that expect sample locations can run without modification. A common misconception is that manual downloads are sufficient — automated scripts that use cURL and Git are repeatable and reduce the risk of mismatching sample versions. Finally, if you plan to share code or collaborate, learning basic Git operations like clone, branch and commit will save time and reduce merge conflicts when working with chaincode and client applications. cURL and Git: download and code management means use curl for scripted downloads and git to clone and manage fabric-samples and your chaincode repositories for reproducible development.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Overall, invest a little time to set up an IDE and ensure your OS packages are current — this reduces incidental errors unrelated to Fabric itself. Editor / IDE

Use an editor with language support and an integrated terminal. Features like linting and debugger extensions accelerate chaincode development and client debugging.

screens.title: Common installation pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How to recognize and fix the most frequent setup errors

narration.text: Several recurring problems tend to block Fabric developers early. One is a missing PATH entry: a tool might be installed but not on your PATH, causing a 'command not found' error. The fix is to locate the binary and add its directory to your shell profile so commands are available in new terminals. Another frequent issue is the Docker daemon not running — the binary exists but the service must be started or enabled. On some systems you must add your user to a docker group or use elevated privileges. For Go, an unset or incorrect GOPATH triggers build errors; set GOPATH to a workspace directory and add GOPATH/bin to PATH. For Node, installing Node without npm or using a broken install method can leave npm unavailable. Always use recommended installers for your platform. A useful troubleshooting approach is to run the version checks in sequence, capture outputs, and then address the first failing tool before moving on. This avoids chasing symptoms caused by an earlier missing component. The goal is a mindset: verify, capture evidence, and fix the root cause rather than applying ad hoc fixes.

keyIdea.title: Verify-sequence-fix
keyIdea.text: Work through verification checks in order, capture the first failing output, and fix the root cause rather than patching symptoms.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Common Pitfalls
Symptom → Likely cause
  • "command not found" — PATH not set or binary not installed.
  • Docker errors about daemon — Docker service is not running or user lacks permissions.
  • Go build errors about packages — GOPATH unset or dependencies missing.
  • npm missing — incomplete Node install or PATH issue.
Fix strategy
  1. Run version checks in order and capture outputs.
  2. Address the first failing tool before proceeding to the next.
  3. Document changes to PATH or system services so you can reproduce the setup later.
Pro tip

When asking for help, include the exact version outputs you captured; they often reveal the root cause immediately.

screens.title: Hands-on: Verify your development environment
screens.subtitle: Run the sequence of checks and record their output

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through the verification activity. Open your terminal and run the sequence of checks that confirm each required tool is installed and accessible. Start with Docker checks: a client version query and a command that reports daemon status. If Docker commands fail, start by ensuring the service is running. Next, check Docker Compose for its version. Then run Go version and echo your GOPATH environment variable; if GOPATH is empty, set it to a workspace directory and add its bin to PATH. After that, verify Node and npm versions to ensure JavaScript runtimes and package management are available. Finally, confirm cURL and Git versions so you can download binaries and clone fabric-samples. As you run each command, copy the output into a text file or take screenshots to document success. If a command fails, note the exact error, attempt the basic fix from the troubleshooting checklist, and re-run the check. This sequence reduces ambiguity and gives you reproducible evidence of a working development environment for Fabric. In practical terms, run the sequence of checks and record their output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Troubleshooting examples and fixes
screens.subtitle: Walk through typical errors and practical corrective steps

narration.text: Let’s examine common error scenarios and concrete fixes you will encounter during setup. Scenario one: a terminal reports a missing Compose command. The likely causes are Compose not installed or not on PATH. Fix this by installing Compose per your OS instructions and ensuring the directory with the Compose binary is on PATH. Scenario two: Docker commands report the daemon is not available. On many systems you must start the Docker service or enable it at boot; alternatively, check that your user has permission to use Docker or run commands with elevated privileges while you configure proper group membership. Scenario three: Go builds fail with missing packages. Confirm GOPATH is set and that you ran the appropriate go get or module-based dependency commands for the sample. If npm commands fail, ensure Node was installed correctly and that npm is available on the PATH. In every case, rerun the verification command after applying the fix. The practical habit to develop is to address the first failing check in your sequence, apply one fix, and confirm that the fix resolves the symptom before moving to the next. This prevents fix cascades and simplifies root cause isolation.

keyIdea.title: One-fix, re-check approach
keyIdea.text: Address the first failing verification step, apply a targeted fix, and re-run checks to confirm the issue is resolved before continuing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Troubleshooting
Issue: command not found
Likely caused by a missing binary or PATH not updated. Fix by locating the binary and adding its directory to your shell profile, then open a new terminal and re-check.
Issue: Docker daemon errors
Start the Docker service, ensure it runs, and verify your user permissions. After starting the daemon, re-run the Docker info check to confirm readiness.
Issue: Go build failures
Confirm GOPATH is set and dependencies are available. If using modules, follow the sample instructions. Re-run go build and verify that the compiler finds required packages.
Checklist

Address one failing check at a time, capture outputs before and after fixes, and document steps taken so fixes are repeatable on other machines.

screens.title: Sample assessment & troubleshooting questions
screens.subtitle: Practice reasoning with common exam-style scenarios

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Assessment Practice
Sample question 1

A developer runs a compose up command and receives a message that the command is not found. What is the most likely cause and the corrective steps?

Ideal response
  1. Verify docker-compose version to confirm presence.
  2. Install Compose or add it to PATH if missing.
  3. Rerun the version check to confirm the fix.
Sample question 2

Why is setting GOPATH important when building Go chaincode, and what happens if it is unset?

Ideal response

GOPATH points to the Go workspace where code and binaries are stored. If unset, go get and go build may fail to find packages, preventing compilation of chaincode. Set GOPATH and add its bin to PATH, then re-run the build.

Assessment tip

When answering, describe the verification commands you would run and attach the captured outputs. Demonstrating the diagnostic steps is as important as the final fix.
